speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals

This Bill proposes to place these electric lines again under the jurisdiction* of the Provincial Government. If I read the main clause of the Bill its purpose will be explained:	.

4.	Did Captain Flynn agree to go to France in accordance with said orders, or did he prefer to return to Canada and accept an appointment similar to the one he had in England, with the First Depot Battalion, 2nd Regiment of Quebec, at Quebec?
5.	If so, were there not, on the list of the Department of Militia, officers having seen service in France with the 22nd Battalion and who had made application, and were qualified and well recommended, to be appointed, adjutants of the 22nd Regiment of the Permanent Force?

7.	If Captain Percy Flynn had no service in France, and if he returned to Canada under the conditions mentioned in question No. 3, after a number of years in England, is it the intention of the Government to continue him as adjutant of the 22nd, or will the Departmeht of Militia consider the appointment of a former officer of the 22nd, having had service on the firing line in France, as adjutant?
8.	Is it the policy of the Government and the Department of Militia to give a preference

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: to officers having had service in France who desire to serve in the Permanent Force of Canada, or are all officers placed on the same footing as those who have only seen service in England, Canada or in Siberia?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
1.	The appointment of Captain Percy Flynn as adjutant of the 22nd Regiment is in a draft gazette dated the 29th April, which has been submitted to the Privy Council for approval.
2.	He did not see service in France.
3.	This officer was appointed a lieutenant
in the 57th Overseas Battalion in May, 1915, and received promotion to the rank of captain on appointment as adjutant on the 19th January, 1916. He proceeded overseas on the 2nd June, 1916. During his period of service overseas he held the following appointments:	Transferred to the
69th Battalion, 8th June, 1916; appointed assistant adjutant, 21st June, 1916; appointed adjutant, 1st July, 1916; transferred to the 10th .Reserve Battalion, 4th January, 1917; appointed adjutant, 8th January, 1917, which appointment he relinquished on the 29th April, 1918, to return to Canada. The services of Captain Flynn were specially applied for by the General Officer Commanding Military District No. 5, Quebec, in February, 1918, as an experienced officer was necessary to undertake the duties of adjutant of the 1st Depot Battalion, 2nd Quebec Regiment, Quebec, and Captain Flynn was considered to be the best officer for the appointment. His return to Canada was, therefore, approved, and he reported for duty on the 22nd May, 1918. He was subsequently appointed to the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Siberia) and served in Siberia from December, 1918, to (May, 1919, as a company commander.
4.	It is true that officers were called upon to revert to the rank of lieutenant to proceed to France, and the records show that Captain Flynn, on the 25th October, 1917, applied to revert accordingly, and that he was compulsorily retained until he could be suitably replaced as adjutant of the 10th Reserve Battalion by a French Canadian overseas casualty. The records further show that these conditions prevailed until the return of Captain Flynn to Canada was approved by special request referred to in paragraph 3. Under the circumstances, it was not considered that his lack of service in France should debar him from permanent military employment.
5.	A list of applicants for appointment to the 22nd Regiment, a number of whom

served with the 22nd Overseas Battalion in France, is on file in the department.
6.	Twenty-five applications .for appointment to the permanent force have been received from officers who served with the 22nd Battalion in France.
7.	This department concurred in the appointment of Captain Flynn as adjutant of the 22nd Regiment owing to the special requests and recommendations of Lieutenant-Colonel H. Chasse, D.S.O., M.C., and of the General Officer Commanding Military District No. 5, after consideration of the names of all officers who had applied, and having regard to his excellent qualifications for the appointment, this department sees no reason for making any change, providing Captain Flynn continues to prove himself an efficient officer as in the past.
8. speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed from May 12, consideration in committee of Bill No. 12 (Hon. Mr. Guthrie) respecting the election of members of the House of Commons and the Electoral Franchise.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When progress was reported upon this Bill on Wednesday last, paragraph (k) of clause 2, clauses 32, 63 and 101 had been allowed to stand. All of the other clauses had been agreed to with the exception of clauses 19 and 76, which cannot be adopted until the House has concurred in the required money resolution. Clause 32 had been discussed at length and was still before the committee. Shall clause 32 carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Since this matter was last before the committee I have had the benefit of !a conference with some of my hon. friends opposite with regard to clause 32, in an effort to carry out, if possible, the suggestions made by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), and other hon. gentlemen opposite. As a result of that conference, I have prepared certain amendments to clause 32, which amendments will, I think, generally speaking, pretty fully meet the suggestions made, although perhaps not in every case to the letter. If the amendments prepared to clause 32 are adopted, the result will be briefly this. In any province of Canada where there is a provincial voters' list not more than two years old, that list shall be adopted as the basis of the Dominion franchise. In cities, towns and villages, or in what are known as urban polling divisions, the procedure laid down in schedule A to the Bill as drawn, will be very nearly followed, there being a few minor amendments to schedule A. But in all rural polling divisions the procedure has been somewhat changed. The provincial list, if not more than two years old, will be accepted as final and complete for rural polling subdivisions, with two provisions, first, that a person may still apply under section 63 of t-he Act to be added on election day and may vote; second, that a person who is not on the provincial polling list may apply to the revising officer of an urban division in the same electoral district to have his name added, and the revising officer is given power to add that name and to notify the

returning officer that the name has been added to the list. Therefore, there will be a double remedy to anybody who has been left off the provincial list and who is a resident of a rural polling division. First, he may go to the poll on election day, be vouched for by two electors who can swear to his qualifications, obtain his ballot and vote. Secondly, he need not wait for election day; he can go directly to the revising officer, have his case determined and have his name added to the list. There is this further provision, that if the revising officer refuses to add his name, after hearing and inquiring into the case, that man shall not subsequently on polling day be entitled to go to the poll and swear himself on. If he does that, we have provided a penalty. The committee will note that the result is this. In a city, town or village, or in a division having cities, towns or villages, the procedure is unchanged and schedule A will prevail. In rural divisions, the procedure is radically changed where there are provincial voters' lists. If there be in existence in any province no provincial voters' lists of less than two years of age since last finally revised and completed, the whole list shall be made in both rural and urban divisions, in urban divisions under schedule A, and in rural divisions under schedule B. This matter was discussed at the conference which we held on Thursday last, and the proposals -seemed to meet with the approval of those present. I have heard that one or two minor objections have since been raised, but the amendments which I have now the honour of moving have been drawn on the basis which I have just outlined. They will involve a considerable amendment to both the schedules of section 32 and a slight amendment to section 33.

What will be the
machinery for adding the names of women who are not on the provincial lists in the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
They will go on either
by application to the revising officer or by application to -the deputy returning officer on polling day. I appreciate the point raised by my hon. friend. Personally, I favoured the old arrangement whereby a rural register would be appointed and would see that all the women as well as the men who were entitled to vote were put on the list, thereby avoiding unnecessary expense. It was put to me most squarely on the ground that where there are lists it would be an unnecessary expense to appoint enumerators throughout Canada for rural polling 
divisions when you had these two safety valves-section 63, as well >as an application to the judge. Under the amendment as now proposed women or men who are not on the provincial list will have to apply in either one of the two ways I have indicated.

I have listened with great interest to the minister's explanation of the amendments. While I have every confidence in the members who assisted the minister in drafting these amendments, I must say that it is hard to appreciate offhand their significance under the new conditions. In the province of Quebec all the women will have to be placed on the list. In the rural divisions they can have their names put on the list, under this new amendment, by applying to the returning officer. How long is he going to sit?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Five days.
How many revising officers will there be for each constituency?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In every urban division there will be one registrar up to a population of 4,000, and an additional registrar for each additional 4,000. Under 1,000, of course, it is a rural division. One revising officer is appointed for each electoral list. He is the county judge and has power to appoint as many additional -as -may be necessary.

It seems, then, that the
women will be obliged to travel a long distance to have their names registered.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They will have to travel to the poll in -any event, and they can vote on polling day without going to the judge.

The difficulty will be this.
There will be 300 electors to each poll. Now it has been said, and with good reason, that it is rather hard to poll 300 votes in one -day in one division, though it can probably be done when all the machinery has been set in order in advance; but if every woman voter has to bring along two witnesses on polling day who will prove that she has a right to vote, that procedure will take some time, and I submit that it will be absolutely impossible for all the women to vote within the time set, on account of the unavoidable delay which this procedure will entail. I think that objection should strike the mind of the minister. It is easy to -calculate how many minutes each person will have to vote when 300 voters have to vote within a certain time, and a calculation will show that the time allowed for each is very limited. There are

bound to be periods during the day when no voters are coming forward, and if there is a crowd of women coming to be sworn in at the end of the day, it will be absolutely impossible for them all to vote under the procedure I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I was of the same opinion as my hon. friend. I preferred the Bill as originally drawn, but these amendments have been drawn to meet the objections of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) and my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau), who pointed out that in cities in the province of Quebec the lists were prepared only once in two years. I do not hink it is possible to meet every suggestion, or to meet everybody's convenience. You cannot grant just as much convenience as you would like in a matter of this kind. The voters have to put themselves out some. However, I do not anticipate even in the case as stated by my hon. friend, that there would be very great difficulty in polling all the votes. A ten-hour day for 300 voters would allow each voter two minutes each, which is more than the average voter takes. Then as a rule they do not all vote. The voters have also another way of getting their names put on the list, by going to the judge, and that would no doubt be done by those who found it convenient to do so. I think that the greater number of those who applied to the deputy returning officer on polling day would be able to vote. I do not mean to say that this is a perfect scheme, but it is the best we have been able to evolve.
May I ask the minister to give his reasons for not having an up-to-date list in the rural districts as well as in the cities?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Under these proposals
it will be just as up-to-date in the rural districts as in the city districts. If there is a provincial voters' list not more than two years old, itt will be adopted, and there is power to add to or strike off that list.
The revising officer is a judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. That would be an up-to-date list. As the Bill was drawn, there was no provision for a revision in the country; it was considered that it would involve too much trouble, because people would have to come to the cities, and it might involve too much work for the revising officer. It was thought that if you adopted the provincial list and gave the individual the right to apply personally to get on that list, or to go to the polls on polling 154
day and be sworn in and vote, you would have an up-to-date list for people who desired to vote, at all events.

In Quebec the names of
women are not on the provincial lists, whereas in Ontario they have been put on the lists. I was not at the conference on Thursday, but as I understand the proposed amendment, application has to be made in person, to the revising officer to be put on the list. Am I right?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I gave you a copy of the amendment. I do not remember the precise wording at the moment.
It does not absolutely say so in so many words. I have not had much time to study it carefully, but I think that is the effect. That was not the case under the Bill as originally drawn.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
To apply in person to
the revising officer.

If it does, I can make the suggestion more pointed. Under the Bill as introduced a voter was entitled to be put on the list by the registrar upon the evidence of a credible person; that was the proposal until this amendment was suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Have you any objection to that being followed out?
As far as the revising officer is concerned? [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, to the Bill as originally drafted.

Yes, because there is- no appeal to the registrar. If it was right to have the registrar, who is to some extent a partisan officer-I do not care what government is in power, whether Liberal or Tory -put on the list a voter on representations made to him by a credible person, why, should it not be right for a judicial officer, without asking the personal appearance of that person, to put on the list the name of a man or woman on similar evidence being offered to him? If the argument was strong in that case, and the original Act was right, it surely would be stronger in this case when the revision is being made by a judicial officer.
I may say that I was not at the conference on Thursday. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) has gone a long way and has been very generous in this whole matter. But under the amendment he suggests applying to the province of Ontario, this sit-

uation arises. As the law of the province now stands, lists are prepared for October, 1919, and if the two-year limitation is left in the Act as it is-and I have no objection to that-on the 20th of October, 1921, there will be no provincial list available, and under the suggested amendment of my hon. friend on the 20th of October, 1921, we in the province of Ontario will have to revert to this veTy thing that we are eliminating for two years. Well, if it is good to eliminate the appointment of registrars and the expense attendant thereon for two years, it is good to eliminate them after the two years.
I suggested to my hon. friend this morning an amendment along these lines, drafted by Mr. Biggar, and I think he will be able to work it in properly.
If in the province of Ontario-
This would apply after two years had gone by. I think it should be made to apply now generally.
-no lists have been prepared and completed as aforesaid,-
That is, within two years.
-but municipal lists are required by law to be annually prepared and to include all persons who could be entitled to vote under this Act at the date of their preparation, the last of such lists shall be used as the voters' list for such election-
What does that mean? I suggest that the municipal lists in Ontario as prepared by the municipal authorities under the provincial laws, and which are prepared every year and include the names of all persons who are entitled to vote under this Act, shall be the basis of the Dominion Elections Act; but there shall be added thereto and subtracted therefrom the names which should be added thereto or subtracted therefrom under this Act in the manner my hon. friend has suggested in his amendment. But if he will not- concur in that, I would suggest that he put in the Act the amendment that has been drafted just casually-I do not say it is agreed to or anything like that-by Mr. Biggar to the effect I have mentioned. Because if he does not do that by October, 1921-although we will have complete municipal lists which will be almost man for man and woman for woman the last lists we want fo' Dominion purposes-in the province of Ontario we are thrown back on the appointment of registrars to prepare new lists at a cost of half a million dollars a year. As I say, if it is good up to 1921 it is good after 1921, and I would ask my hon. friend 
in all fairness and as a matter of economy to have that suggested amendment made.
Is it not a fact that the municipal lists in Ontario are based upon a property qualification? How could you make use of that?

Under the Bill introduced by Premier Drury and which is before the Ontario Legislature at the present time,-and which, I have no doubt, will he passed before this Parliament rises-the system of making up the municipal lists is being entirely changed. At the time of the last election the enumeration system was adopted and found to work very unsatisfactorily, thousands of men being left off the lists and the expense being very heavy, over $500,000, as I pointed out the other day. But the Ontario Government is now passing a law that every man and woman twenty-one years of age shall be put on the assessment roll, and the assessment roll is made the basis of the voters' list, consequently the voters' list prepared by the municipality are just as complete a basis as can possibly be secured for federal election.
But that Bill may be changed in the same way as this Bill has been changed; it has not passed the Legislature yet.
That is true; but even if it is changed, all that will mean will be that the revising officer will have a little more work to do-a few more names to add; it cannot mean anything else.

With regard to the Nova Scotia lists about which there was some controversy, I am glad to bje able to say that the proposals made by the hon. minister (Mr. Guthrie) go very far to remove the objections which I ventured to offer. You will remember, Mr. Chairman, that I tried to picture the Nova Scotia lists as [DOT] so safe and sound that they could be accepted in their entirety. The Bill departed from them in two points. In urban districts it provided for an appeal to the county judge, which is retained in the Bill as it now stands. While I thought that was unnecessary, I have no objection. Our chief difficulty, however, was in regard to the rural lists; there it was proposed that the Nova Scotia lists under the provincial law should be revised by officials called registrars. I am glad to note that the minister, for various reasons, one being the large expense throughout the Dominion, has withdrawn the provision regarding registrars. He has.

retained, however, this safeguard, that if there are any persons who feel that they have been improperly left off the Nova Scotia lists, they shall have the right to appear at the polls and by there swearing on qualify themselves. As I have already said, I do not like the idea of a man swearing himself on the list on election day. However, the minister has guarded that by the amendment that he has made, and I do not think there is any very serious objection to be urged now. I want to say with regard to elimination of the registrars, that the minister has gone a long way to meet Our wishes, and I hope on other grounds we will be able to come to an understanding. On the Quebec and Ontario lists I must refrain from expressing any opinion, because I have not given so much attention to those as to the lists of my own province.

In all Franchise Acts at present, both provincial and Dominion, special provision is made for the unorganized districts in any province. According to this Act no special provision is made so far as I have been able to discover. I would point out to the minister in charge of the Bill that lists two years old are as a rule absolutely useless in an unorganized territory. The ordinary voters in a mining or lumbering district almost entirely change in the course of two years, and this mode of preparation as suggested by the amendment would practically annul all such lists. There is also this to be considered, that in many cases these lists being in existence, polls will be held in subdivisions where there will be absolutely no voters at the time of the election. On the other hand, the men- who had been voters in those polling divisions will have moved to some Other part of the constituency, or to another constituency, in which they would have no chance to be placed on any of the lists. I think this matter should have the consideration of the minister before pressing the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I realize that in unorganized districts where there are no municipal institutions there is more difficulty in regard to the voters lists.

There is no difficulty
under the system of registration.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I would like to see a list prepared in unorganized districts within thirty days if it were possible, but that breaks the rule we are applying to the rest of Canada. We must try to have a uniform 1641
system. I have had to tell my hon. friends from Quebec that we cannot make a special provision for Quebec; they must be put to some inconvenience too. If one is going to make an Act to bring every convenience to the door of everybody it is going to be a very difficult thing to frame one that will in the end be practicable. Objections have been raised from the province of Ontario to this arrangement by the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) and objections have been raised to the arrangement on behalf of the provinces of Nova iScotia and New Brunswick. I 'see the difficulty pointed out by my hon. friend from Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs). If we cannot adopt something that is going to he of general application I do not see anything to do but to make a uniform law and stick to the proposition originally drafted even although it would involve heavy expense. The proposals I make are not made on my own behalf or on behalf of the Government but they are proposals made to meet the objections raised by hon. gentlemen opposite. If they are not satisfied with them there is no use of going on with a proposition that pleases nobody and displeases everybody. I would rather hear a little further discussion before coming to a conclusion; I do not wish to impose my will on the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The main purpose of the conference, as I understood it was to see if it were possible to avoid the duplication and the great expense involved in the prepartion of voters1 lists where lists are already prepared and are satisfactory. Each one can speak best in reference to his native province. The present proposal refers particularly to the province of Ontario. The Ontario Government is putting through a law which will require that every year lists shall be made up in every municipality urban an rural, which list will include the name of every man and woman who is entitled to vote.- These lists will be made up year after year. What we ask is that these lists, with the prepartion of which Ottawa has nothing to do, they toeing prepared by the municipality, shall be taken as the basis of the voters lists for federal purposes. If the law stands as it is at present all this work will be done by the Provincial Government, but in addition to that the minute we propose to have a federal election the Dominion Government will have to appoint an army of enumerators to go over the province of Ontario to prepare fresh lists disregarding those lists which

are perfect in themselves. This is an enormous waste of money.

We
have to do that in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The cost at
the last election ran up to half a million dollars or more. Why should that amount be soent to produce lists less satisfactory? The. question that has arisen with regard to Ontario arises from the fact that we are not certain just when the provincial lists will be completed and what my hon. friend from West Middlesex desires is simply to make certain that there will not be under this Act the expense of the double preparation of the voters' lists. :I think that was also the purpose in regard to the other provinces such as New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Where these lists exist the idea is to use them as the basis of the federal franchise and to save the enormous expense involved in the preparation of new lists.

In view of the statement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) I must say that my question as to the *means of putting women on the lists in the provinces where they have no vote was not intended as a criticism of the amendment. I very much prefer the amendment to the clause as it stands in the Bill. I think we should do away with this enumerator business altogether. My hon. friend need not say that he will withdraw the amendment because we have criticized it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It was not on that account I made that remark but it looked to me as if the amendment did not please hon. members on either side of the House.
Mr. 'LAPOINTE:	I like it better than
the clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
My objection to my
hon. friend's statement in regard to the Ontario lists is this: I do not think it a proper thing to make a patchwork of the election law, and that we should have one law for one province and another law for another province. If we cannot get some kind of uniformity we had better stick to the old law. We should have a uniform franchise law and a uniform method of carrying on our elections. The hon. member for West Middlesex and the hon. the leader of the Opposition both take the ground that it may possibly be that in the course of time we will have municipal lists which will suit our purpose, but they cannot give the assurance that that will be so. The hon. member for West Middlesex

is hugging a Bill-I have not had the opportunity of examining it-and he says that the Drury Government is going to do so and so. It has not done it yet. As a matter of fact in the province of Ontario we have the provincial voters' lists prepared last fall still in force, and if this House dissolved to-day those voters' lists would be the basis of the lists that we would have to use. It is beneath our dignity to wait on the Drury Government and see what they are going to do. They will probably change the law; it may be amended and reamended. When they see what we have adopted they may meet our suggestions. I cannot see any sense or reason in the suggestion that because a Bill has been introduced into the Ontario Legislature which may or may not ultimately suit the case, we should deliberately drop something we believe to be the best suited to carry out the purpose in view in order to meet some policy which they may adopt in the Ontario Legislature and which they may undo two or three weeks hence. In regard to Nova Scotia, I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) that the object to be attained there was the avoidance of expense and duplication of effort, and that it was possible for us to do that for the simple reason that they have provincial lists there just as they have in British Columbia, where they have an annual preparation of voters' lists. In Quebec they have one every two years.
Every year.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Every year in the rural parts, but every two years in the large cities.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
We are changing the
clause as originally drawn from one year to two years bo meet the case of the cities in the province oif Quebec, but we give it general application throughout Canada and the whole of the clause has been drawn to that end. No matter whether it is Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, or any other province that has a provincial list, we adopt, that list. I am not going to make exceptions. I do not counsel the making of exceptions for different provinces. I do not think it would be wise or fair to do so, and if the amendment is not going to be better received on both sides of the House than it has been I am satisfied it is going to disappoint a great many people. That-is the reason I would like to have the matter more fully discussed. I do not want to have it condemned, because there is merit

in it, but if we are going to add to it, to take from it, and re-write the whole thing, why let it go.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I say to my hon. friend that we are not taking any exception for the purpose of having an amendment which would be generally applicable; the point we are raising at the moment is simply one of interpretation to carry out the spirit of the amendment. The purpose of the amendment being to use, if possible, the lists that are in existence, we simply want to make sure that if those lists are in existence they will be used and that they will not be lost sight of altogether through failure to draw the attention of the Government to a possible consequence of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is a very grave exception to draw an amendment to provide that in the province of Ontario we shall accept the municipal lists, because if at the next session of the legislature of the province they change their method of getting up the provincial lists we shall be all away from it. Then we would have adopted the Ontario municipal lists, and the legislature would have provided for new provincial lists.

I do not think my hon.
friend quite understood the purport of my suggested amendment, although doubtless he appreciates the spirit in which I made it; it was only to carry out what I understood was the conclusion arrived at in the conference on Thursday. Now the suggested amendment which I made was this: The time may arrive when more than two years may elapse and there will be no provincial list.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: But there is a provincial list.

I know that as well as my hon. friend does. However, I do not want to get into a controversy with him. I admit he has been very generous in trying to meet these cases, but I am only pointing out that there is one little point that he has not meant by his amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have met the only
case I tried to meet. I never agreed-and never heard it suggested until to-day-to adopt the provincial list.

I am not saying that the hon. gentleman is not correct, I am only pointing out a situation which may arise. Supposing election does not take place until two years from last October. There will then be no up-to-date provincial lists in
force. The amendment I suggested was simply this: If in Ontario the provincial legislature enacts that municipal lists shall be prepared annually-which we think they will enact-and that on all such lists the name shall appear of the persons who are entitled to vote under our Dominion Franchise Act-if that happens and the provincial lists are more than two years old then the municipal lists containing all the names of the electors that are entitled to be on them under the Dominion Franchise Act that we are enacting to-day shall be taken as a basis and names added thereto or subtracted therefrom according to the very plan my hon. friend has set out. I will frankly admit that the amendments my hon. friend has made are a great improvement on the original Bill, and we appreciate them very much. It may be the suggestions that I have made are not good, but I am not making them in any spirit of opposition. I am advancing them in the hope, if possible, of still further improving the Bill and saving expense, a thing we all admit would be a wise procedure. That is the whole object of my suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: In the preparation of the municipal lists by the municipal authorities each year will the names of persons be included regardless of whether or not they had the proper qualification?

My hon. frieend has put a
very fair question and in reply to him I will read the clause from the Ontario Bill. It is section eighty-six, which reads as follows :
In addition to the particulars required by The Assessment Act, to be entered upon the assessment roll, every assessor shall enter upon the roll the name of every person who is of the full age of twenty-one years, a British subject, and who has been a resident of Ontario for a period of nine months-
In this Bill the period is nine months, but I believe an amendment has been adopted to provide that the period shall be twelve months

-prior to the date fixed for the assessor to begin to make up his roll, and who is a resident of the municipality and qualified in other respects as the assessor believes, to vote at elections to the Assembly.
My hon. friend will see how broad this provision is. It applies to every person twenty-one years of age, who is a British subject, who has resided in Ontario for nine, or twelve months, and who is a resident of the county.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
That being the case what is the provision of the proposed law in so far

as regards making that the provincial list at the time of the election?

L will explalin to my hon. friend: That is the (basis of the provincial . list, and once a dissolution of the provincial House, or a vacancy dn the Assembly, occurs in an indiivlidual city, an election board, consisting of the county judge and four other persons, sits and takes that list as .a basis. In each muniicipalilty they take that liist and add to, or strike off, the names of persons who -are entitled to vote for a member of the legislature. But the Bill of my hon. Mend (Mr. Guthrie), with suggested amendments, has provided just as efficient machinery whereby that list can be taken 'as a basis and by the. revising officer-for whose appointment the Bill provides-namep can be added to, or struck off the list just as in the Ontario Act. We are quite ready to concur in the machinery which my hon. friend has provided except that we would like to see this one suggestion adopted. That suggestion,
I would say, is made in all kindness.
My hon. friend has juist read from a Bill Which has not yet been passed by tire legislature of Ontario.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: That is absolutely true.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend who has just spoken (in regard to the Ontario list, will see the significance of what is in our mind when I mention to him that until the provincial legislature is dissolved there will not be in existence a provincial list for Ontario, although .alii this work of registration will have been completed year after year. The present Government in Ontario may hold office for the next four years, and we recognize that unless some provision of the kind suggested is made the provincial list may not apply at all at the next general election and under the machinery o'f 'the present Bill the lists would have to be prepared by a great army of enumerators, and the advantages that would 'be derived from using the existing lists would be lo^t.
Lists are prepared annually by the municipalities in organized districts, 'but we have unorganized districts in Northern Ontario, and I presume also in Northern Quebec.
No.

There are large numbers of voters whose names would not be on any municipal list, and if it is incumbent that

they should appear liin person before >the revising officer in order to have their nam.es added to the voters' lists it would mean in some cases their travelling three hundred or three hundred land fifty miles for that purpose. Therefore I think we should consider such a provision very carefully before we adopt it.

I must say that I am absolutely opposed to the adoption, as a basis for our own lists, of a provincial list that may be two years old, and I am opposed to adopting a municipal list, leaving it to be revised in the manner that is suggested. Any man who, has had experience in connection with the preparation of muni-dipal lists knows that there is not a municipality in the province of Ontario-or in any dther province for that matter, where the assessor makes up the list-where there are not scores of voters left off every list. Now, in order to have 'those voters placed on the list one of two ways is open to you: First, .an appeal may be made to the registrar, who may be ten or twenty mites away. You ask the individual voter to appear in person before the registrar in order to have his name placed on the list, and two citizens must -accompany him to the poll and also take an oath. Otherwise that man cannot cast his ballot. I have seen sixty names taken off the list in a poll of less than three hundred-and that a list which had been prepared the same year. Now, if you have twenty or thirty people coming to a poll who must be sworn, each with two or three others who must be sw-orn, you will never be able to poll all the votes. At the last election, in polls of two hundred and fifty or three hundred, or more, it was found difficult to get the votes polled-during the prescribed hours, even though only an occasional person had to be sworn. A federal franchise should be a federal franchise, independent of the provincial, municipal or any other authority. Surely Canada as a whole is sufficiently interested in the election of members to the House of Commons to be willing to bear the expense of having an up-to-date voters' list. In the past we have had the experience of one province having one law and another another. I remember when one man could vote two or three times in one province and eoiild only vote once in another. Hon. members from Quebec know that it is only a few years since men in their province could, if they had the property qualifications, vote in as many different polls and in as many different
I

places as they could get around to in the hour.
But in different ridings.

I know, but it was
the case of one man voting two or three times, whereas in another province one man could vote only once.

Of course, he had to be
qualified in each riding.

We used to have a
similar law in Ontario, but we changed it and adopted the principle of one man one vote. I believe in the principle of one man one vote, one woman one vote, all over Canada, and that we should have an up-to-date list-a list which is right up to the minute.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think that
this point we are now discussing in regard to Ontario' really need not have been raised at all, if we have in mind what took place in debate here before the matter was discussed in committee. In the conference we were simply seeking to give expression to what had been said on the floor of Parliament in regard to Ontario by the Acting Solicitor General himself. Let me read from Hansard, page 2430. The question in our minds was as regards the application of the Ontario lists, and I asked the Acting Solicitor General at the time:
Assuming that the Ontario law were now passed and that lists were prepared under it by November or December of this year; then those lists would be used?
Mr. Guthrie: They would be valid for twelve months.
Now, that was the impression we all had at the conference. That was the impression that I think every one had until this morning, when my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) pointed out that a different construction of the Ontario law might leave us in the position of having no Ontario lists until the provincial House bad dissolved. Well, that was a situation that we had never contemplated, either in discussion here, when we decided to have a conference, or during the conference itself. All that we are suggesting at the moment is that if possible we give expression to what was in our minds, not at the conference but in the committee when this matter was discussed the other night, namely that we use for federal purposes lists that have already been prepared and concerning which there can be no question.

I am not quite so clear about the things that are to be done under this Ontario Bill as the leader of the Opposition seems to be. We do not know what the law of Ontario is going to be; moreover, no matter what it is going to be, no matter what it does when finally passed, we have no control over legislation respecting the Ontario franchise or qualifications for voters. There is really involved in this question the thought of what an interesting and difficult situation might arise in the changing views of parties in the Ontario legislature. There is a suggestion from some hon. members that we want to avoid expense. I think every hon. member desires to avoid unnecessary expense, but after all I do not think that we should throw too much expense upon the individual, upon the people at large. That is what the suggestion which has been made would do; it would put every person who is unfortunate enough to be off the list under the obligation of travelling, perhaps, some distance at considerable expense in order to make personal application to have his name put on, and to prosecute appeals, and so on; and upon voting at polling day to bring two neighbours to vouch for him. Here are three oaths; a most complicated piece of machinery, throwing upon the public at large what I conceive ought to be done by the Government-that is, the making of a complete,- definite and up-to-date franchise law under which every one would know that his name was on the list, provided he did not by supineness or neglect fail to reach the forum at home through which he might get his name upon it. It looks to me as if the tail were wagging the dog. May I throw out the suggestion to hon. gentlemen that we are really engaged in drafting a franchise law for the whole Dominion? The franchise is a valuable right concerning which the public at large are zealous as well as jealous, and it is the duty of this Parliament to make out a proper list, no matter what the expense may be. Under the Bill as proposed, a part of the expense, it is true, will be avoided in the case of those provinces which have lists. If every province had a list-and I do not see why they should not -the work would be largely done, and, if it was properly done, the only additional expense would be that involved in picking up the few persons who had failed to get on the provincial lists. I do not think that the suggestion of expense involved in bringing that about may be looked upon as an insuperable difficulty. Take Prince Edward

Island as a case in point. They have no lists at all. A man walks up to the polling booth and presents his qualifications in the shape of having paid his poll tax, or otherwise; he votes, even though there never was a list upon which his name could be put. I do not know how far I should be right in saying that it is worth while having a list in Prince Edward Island, but it seems to me that if every province were listed either by this Parliament or by the local legislature, there would be a tendency to bring the situation to a finality. But to put upon the individual here and there who is left off the list the onus and the extreme expense of getting his name on does not appeal to me as a democratic way of dealing with the public who desire the franchise. Surely this Government is big enough to carry out its own' franchise laws. In fact, we were pretty well agreed in this regard until my hon. friend (Mr. Ross) threw a monkey wrench into the machinery and brought on this discussion. I am satisfied that if the provincial lists were to follow this legislation instead of our following provincial legislation, as hon. gentlemen opposite want us to do, a solution of the whole question would be found.
We were very close to having a list that would be satisfactory to all hon. members; but the hon. member (Mr. Ross), as the Acting Solicitor General says, hugging to himself a Bill that is not a Bill, an Act that is not an Act, an Act that may to-morrow be abandoned altogether and not passed, would put this Parliament into the position of following the arguments founded upon that flimsy basis, and of passing legislation that would not be operative at all because either of the failure of that Bill to be passed, or, if it be passed, later on to be changed, thus throwing all the machinery out of gear.

I did not intend to throw
any monkey wrench into the machinery at all, and I do not think I have done so. My hon. friend will see that I did not say that this Act had been passed or was going to be passed or that any other Act was going to be passed. My suggested amendment is entirely hypothetical; it may be operative or it may not. If certain things occur, it will become operative. If in Ontario no lists have been prepared and completed as aforesaid, that is, if no provincial lists have been prepared and completed for provincial purposes within the two years, then there is a hiatus and we would have to appoint registrars.

This is based on an "if." I understood my hon. friend was going to say that municipal lists were to be prepared every year.
Mr, ROSS: If my hon. friend will allow me to finish my suggested amendment, I think he will see that my suggestion has some merits. If lists had been prepared and completed, they would be used as aforesaid, but the municipal lists are required by law to be prepared annually and to include all persons who would be entitled to vote under this Act.

That is not the case
at the present time in Ontario, is it?

The present time would not
be affected at all, because provincial lists will be in force for two years from the 20th October, 1919; but if this time should expire and there are no provincial lists in force, and if Ontario, by any accident or by design, should pass this legislation which is now before the legislature, my suggested amendment becomes effective. In that case there is an annual revision by the municipalities and all names which would be on the lists prepared by the House of Commons are put on the municipal lists, and those lists shall be adopted.
If that does not happen, my suggested amendment will not become effective.

We might as well be frank in this matter. The question that is bothering my hon. friends opposite is not one of expense, if we have regard to what transpired in the country when they had control of expenses in the conduct of elections. What is troubling them most now is this, that if we can prevent enumerators from being appointed under this Act, as they would be, going around from house to house and making the enumeration and using their influence, as was done in the West when the provincial elections were held, it is the desire of the Opposition to prevent that as far as they possibly can. My hon. friend (Mr. Ross) has nothing other in view than the fact that an enumerator appointed by the Government has an opportunity of going from individual to individual and imposing his personal views upon him, and if the enumerator is an appointee of the Government, he has a certain amount of influence. That is the objection raised by the Opposition, but it is not stated, as a fact.

Is it not a good objection?
(Mr. MACKIE (East Edmonton): Yes it is a good one, but what is practised upon me in my province, I want to practise upon the other fellow. I am willing to be imbued with a Christian spirit to a large extent, but not to the extent of turning the other cheek to the enemy. In a constituency such as I represent, which is 700 miles long by an average of 150 wide. I take the provincial list that has been prepared by the enumerators of the Alberta Government, and who is going to tell me at Fort Chipewyan or at Fort Smith, five or six hundred miles away from Edmonton, who should be on that list? Are you going to place on me the onus of sending men up there at a cost of five or six hundred dollars each to check up that list for me and find out whether all the Indians have been put on ' it or not. If the provincial lists were prepared to my satisfaction in an honest manner, I would be quite willing to accept them; but I know how elections are run in Alberta, and you would adopt the provincial lists of Alberta, because in 1923 or in the fall of 1922 the Provincial Government must go to the people, and I assume, unless there is something that I do not know of in the federal law, this Government must also go to the people before 1923. In that case we would be within the two year period when we are bound to accept the provincial lists such as they are. It is all right to speak about revision, but who is going to look after and pay for it? Some time ago I gave in this House an instance where men's names had been placed on the list, and the last night before the deputy returning officer gets the lists for the poll, the enumerator who made the list has power under the law to erase every one of those names from the list. It is a noted fact to-day that, as a result of what has been practised in our province, people are applying by the hundreds to this Government for naturalization papers. Why? Because during the election these people were given naturalization application papers. They believed they were naturalized; they were put on the list, and they voted. Are we going to accept this list? Am I to be responsible for going around- every Ruthenian community in my constituency to find out if everybody is properly on the list or not? I would rather have an enumerator go around and do that work, even if he uses his influence, because if so, that is exactly what has been practised upon us in that province for the last few years. Let my hon. friends opposite
admit that they do not want these enumerators because they are afraid that these enumerators are part and parcel of a machinery that will be used against them. Then we shall be able to deal with my hon. friends.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As regards the enumerators, let me be perfectly frank. I feel the electorate generally has not the same confidence in a list prepared by enumerators as in a list prepared in the regular way for municipal and provincial purposes ard serving also federal purposes. If we can, in working on this measure, do anything which will help to bring about in Canada a system of preparation of lists which will serve for municipal, provincial and federal purposes, we shall be rendering a service to all three organized groups. As my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy) said, that was the thought that was in our minds at the conference the other day, coupled with *an endeavour to give expression to what had been virtually agreed on between the two sides in the previous evening's discussion. I would suggest that we consider the amendments which the minister has introduced, in the light of what he himself has in mind, namely, framing something that will be applicable to the whole Dominion without exception one way or another. That is the basis on which we should proceed. After we have adopted the general suggestion, we might consider whether we should go further than that and add some amendments to meet a condition that is temporary, and that will exist possibly only for the next year or two. But to throw aside what is of general application simply because there has been brought to the attention of the committee a circumstance that has a bearing on one province for one election, would, I think, be a great mistake and very unfortunate.
Because it may be favourable to Ontario or Quebec to adopt a certain method, is that any reason why I should support that method when it is objectionable to me?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Not at all.

Then
make my province an exception. I do not want the provincial list, and I am going to vote against this amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think in the province of Alberta the lists are prepared by the system of enumeration, and the suggestion that is now being made will not apply to that province at all.

But if a Dominion election is held within two years after a provincial election, the provincial lists form the basis of the Dominion lists, and I must accept those lists whether they have been prepared correctly or not. If I were a candidate in the same constituency, I would be put to the trouble and expense of going to every individual on that list to find out whether he was properly on the list, and whether men who were entitled to be on the list had ben left off. Who is going to pay for that? Suppose theTe was no provincial list: I am entitled to my enumeration, anyhow. But in the case of a Dominion election toeing held within two years after a provincial election, I am bound to accept the provincial lists as a basis for the Dominion lists, and I would have to have enumerators going from one place to another throughout a constituency 700 miles by 150 to ascertain whether these lists were properly made up. I say the Government should pay for that. If I have to do it in the next election I shall not run, because I have not the money to do it.

I want to protest against the suggestion that the northern parts of Ontario and the unorganized districts throughout Canada are ashing for special treatment. These unorganized districts have always been accorded special treatment in this regard under the law. The Franchise Bill as introduced provided for a system of registration by enumerators, which was essentially the practice followed in the unorganized territories in the past. So we are asking for no special treatment for these unorganized districts in the preparation of the lists, because that has always been the law.
I would also point out that if the present amendment should carry, it will disfranchise thousands of good citizens in Northern Ontario and other unorganized parts of Canada, and we would also have cases in the unorganized portions where there would not be a single inhabitant in some of the polling divisions. I know divisions in my own riding that had a voting population of 200 upwards, but where when the poll was held next year, there were no voters except the returning officer and the poll clerk. The men who had been in that polling division had moved away to other parts, and I say that if this amendment is adopted, thousands will be deprived of their vote through having moved away, or they will have to travel a long distance and give up two or three days' time to make a personal appearance before the judge to have their names put on the list. If they took the 
alternative and appeared on polling day to vote, who is there in a mining or lumbering district who -could swear that these men, hundreds of them, were entitled to vote? I say the provision is absolutely unworkable.
I Tepeat, we are not asking for any special treatment for the unorganized portions of Canada, but simply for the franchise law as it has stood on the statute book for years.

I would not like to subscribe to the doctrine enunciated by my hon. friend (Mr. H. A. Mackie). He apparently feels that his party has -been getting the worst of it, by reason of certain actions of Provincial Governments, and he would like to get even with them in Dominion elections. I would not care to endorse that principle.

The
hon. member does not quite understand me. I pointed out what I considered were errors practised by the Povincial Government, and I say you should not force me to adopt the results of those errors. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that we should not have enumerators, because they see an evil in that. It is an evil that has been practised against us. I say that if it is an evil, that is no reason why I should have to adopt the result of that evil. If there is an evil in having enumerators it is only what is practised by the other side.

The hon. gentleman if
struck on the one cheek would not be content to turn the other, but it occurs to me that if this method is not adopted, and you place the making of the lists in the hands of partisans he would possibly be struck on both cheeks at once if a different kind of government came into power in this country. What I rose to say was this: While I appreciate what my hon. friend-(Mr. Arthurs) has said as being perhaps the only valid objection to the suggestion that has been made from this side of the House, I shall support the proposal of the hon. member (Mr. Ross) because I believe we shall thereby get a more complete and a fairer list at less expense. I have no particular complaint to make so far as the elections of 1917 are concerned with regard to the enumerators in my constituency. They were not perfect, but I have no special complaint to make. I do say this, however: Municipal lists prepared by assessors who ard, we might say, experts in that particular work are almost certain to be more complete and more accurate than lists that are prepared by men who are employed in

many cases, not so much for their ability in that particular work, but perhaps more for partisan purposes. I am not going to make any criticism of that, because no matter what government is in power, whether it be Liberal, Conservative, Unionist, Farmer, or any other, the enumerators are pretty sure to be selected from amongst the Government's own supporters.

If you lived in a province where it was possible for the provincial enumerator to erase as many names off the list as he liked just about six hours before the poll opened, would you be willing to accept that list as a basis for your Dominion list, and be put to the personal expense and trouble of checking the list?
That may be a very fair objection, but the point I was going to make was that the amendment proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Ross) would not affect the province of Alberta at all.
That is quite right.

But as regards the province of Ontario I say the Government would do a great deal better to adopt the lists that are prepared by men who are better qualified than anybody else you could possibly select, than to have the lists prepared by men selected haphazard, according to their partisan affiliations. In the cities you have men appointed as assessors who are reputable in every way, men of ability, and who know practically every citizen in the community. They are not very apt to overlook any one, and as they put names on the list for municipal purposes, it is not likely that they will be governed in the slightest degree by a man's political belief or leanings. I support the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Ross) because I believe it will mean we will get lists that are fairly made up without any reference to a person's political belief, or colour or stripe, or anything of that kind. The case was mentioned here .last week of the enumerators in the city of Toronto who had left
30,000	names off the list. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that could not happen under the aseesors' system. According to fhe amendments submitted by the Acting Solicitor General, provincial lists are to govern if they are not more than two years old. I see no objection why, beyond that time, we should not accept the lists prepared by the assessors. If the Bill now toe-fore the Ontario' Legislature goes through-

Why put the two-year
limitation on at all?

I would be quite satisfied, as far as I am concerned, to change that. But if after the two-year period you want to use lists complete and free from most of the objections that can be urged in political affairs, you cannot do better than accept the lists prepared by the assessors. As far as the other provinces are concerned, I admit that I know very little about their electoral machinery, and there may be very serious objection to the amendment. I think the point mentioned by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) is probably well taken. But if these assessors' lists are taken I think we shall get the best lists available.

I desire to point out one weakness in the proposal of the hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. Ross) supported by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Eluler) in regard to adopting municipal lists. For example, I happen to own property in the city of Fort William and also in the city of Port Arthur, and those cities are in separate constituencies. Consequently my name being on the municipal lists of both cities I could, according to this proposal, vote in both constituencies.
Those municipal lists are to be taken only as a basis. [DOT]

Property owners on the
municipal lists are absolute voters. I go across and vote in Port Arthur at every municipal election and dozens of others do the same.

I do not think it is the
intention that those municipal lists shall be adopted holus bolus; they are simply to serve as a basts.

I quite understand that.
But, for example, take a man on the voters' list in the city of Toronto and also on the voters' list of the city of Hamilton, which is only a short run by automobile, and he may be also on the voters' lists of other municipalities in the neighbourhood-I am not acquainted with their names-he might be on half a dozen voters' lists.
He can practise personation, of course.
It is not a case of personation; he would be voting legally because his name is on the municipal list.
No, he has to vote where he resides.

I vote in the municipal
elections of Port Arthur and of Fort William.

That is quite right.
Mr. MA'NODON:	If the municipal lists
are adopted for the province of Ontario, my name will be on the voters' lists for the two constituencies I have referred to.
Mr. BELAiND:	If my hon. friend is on
two lists, what of it? It is one man one vote.
Then if the municipal lists are adopted, and my name is not struck off either the Fort William or the Port Arthur list, I could vote in the two constituencies.
No.

However, Mr. Chairman, it is quite obvious to any one listening to the discussion that it is impossible to prepare any law to suit every one on both sides of this House. The members of the Opposition have brought up many amendments to the various clauses, and I think the minister in charge of the Bill has been very fair in adopting them, but if he is going to adopt every suggestion from every quarter, we will have to sit here until September. I would like to see a general law adopted that will he as fair as possible to the whole Dominion, but I do not think it is wise for the minister to attempt to satisfy every hon. member.
/-Will my hon. friend say which of the suggestions made by hon. members on this side of the House have been adopted by the other side?
I do not know that I could give them in absolute detail.
I do not know of one to date.

I think objection has
come to a number of clauses from the other side that have been adopted by the minister, and he can give the details.

speechtext:

the time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In order that we may know exactly where we were at the

time of this conference, allow me to remind the House twlha!t was said the other evening as to what had changed the feeling of most of us on this side. When this Bill was first introduced nothing hlad been said about the possibility Of the Ontario Government devising any machinery tor the purpose of preparing election lists. The result was that as we read this Bill it seemed to us that the Government wished to adopt the system of enumeration for the whole Dominion. Once, however, the Ontario Government introduced a Bill which provided machinery for the preparation otf lists, and this Act by remaining as it is, just in the words in which it is at present expressed, indicated that where provincial lists were available those lists would be used, our whole attitude changed, because our objection was, first of all, to this system of enumeration, which we think is thoroughly bad; and, in the second place, to the additional expense of preparing separate lifet.s. On Wednesday evening in speaking to the minister I drew attention to the fiadt that our (attitude had changed, because according to his own interpretation of the Bill, since he introduced it in the House, if there were lists in Ontario prepared by the Ontario Government those would be the lists which -we would use in federal elections. The point that has been raisea to-day through the amendment of my hon. friend from Middlesex (Mr. Ross) as brought to the notice of the House, was not thought of on Friday night, and has not been thought of since, and was not in the mind of the minister (at the time at which we expressed our willingness to accept section 32 a>s it stands, lif it had the inters pretation which we believed it to have. Let me read what was said in debate so that hon. members may see the situation for themselves.
At page 2430, speaking myself, I said:
In order to make clear the effect of the law as it would be if we passed this section,-
That is, section 32 as St stands at the present time.
-let me put a question to the minister.
Assuming that an election were to take place in Canada within a year of the time the Drury Government was formed, that is, before November of this year, then that election would' be held on the lists used in the last provincial election?
Mr. Guthrie: If they were not more than twelve months old.
Mr. Mackenzie King: If an election came before November of this year, the lists used for federal purposes so far as Ontario is concerned would be the lists that were used in the last provincial election. Now if the genera] election

came in December, before the law now being drafted in Ontario, was put into motion, then the lists would be prepared by enumerators in accordance with the provisions of this Act, without any reference whatever to the law that the Ontario Government is putting through at the present time.
Mr. Guthrie: No, unless lists were prepared under that law.
Mr. Mackenzie King: Assuming that the Ontario law were now passed and that lists were prepared under it by November or December of this year then those lists would be used?
Mr. Guthrie: They would be valid for twelve months.
Mr. Mackenzie King: But if they were not prepared until say March or April of next year and a general election took place before then, lists would be prepared under the provisions of this Act?
Mr. Guthrie: Well, I understand that the proposal is that the Ontario Bill shall be passed and that the provincial lists for this year shall be prepared under it. I understand mat they have to be prepared for municipal purposes in any case.
Mr. Mackenzie King: I simply wanted to make the point clear.
Mr. Guthrie: I think that the Ontario law will be in force by December next, anyway. There might be a month or two after November and before the new provincial lists come during which, if a general election were held, we might have to prepare new lists.
Clearly what the minister believed and what he gave the House to understand at that time was that under section 32 as it is tin the Bill now, irrespective of any conference one way or the other, if the Drury Government passes the Bill which is before the Ontario legislature at the present time, which makes provision for lists based on municipal lists prepared toy assessors, those lists would be the lists used for federal elections, provided that those lists were prepared within this next year.
That was the understanding that we had in this House and it was to give effect to that understanding that we had the conference. I drew attention to the fact that the minister's interpretation of the Act as it was expressed made us seem very much closer together than we had believed would have been possible. The reason I say that is that when this Bill was introduced there was no thought of making provision for the use of Ontario lists whereas the use of provincial lists being provided for as matters are at present the complexion of things is changed. If we can consider the amendments which my hon. friend from West Middlesex has suggested as covered by the interpretation which the minister has given to the Ontario Act, I am perfectly satisfied. I do not think +here is any need to go a step further. With reference to the point which my hon. friend has raised, if there is a doubt of any kind we would be negligent if we did not
draw attention to it and suggest the insertion of a subclause which would remove any possibility of doubt. When a matter of a complicated kind is under con- ' sideration men who have the opportunity of sitting down together and thinking only of what is going to be of 'the greatest service to all concerned can perhaps work it out more clearly than can be done in a discussion where we jump from one subjedt to another.
Do the provincial officials have absolute authority in connection with the revising of the provincial lists?

m3
As I understand the matter, under this proposal which has come from this most extraordinary conference, the enumerators are done away with in the "rural districts. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Where there are provincial lists not more than two- years old.

If you adopt this proposal the people in the rural districts are going to be put to a much greater amount of trouble to get on the lists than they would have been subjected to under the original Bill-onuch more trouble. It means that there will be hundreds, yes thousands, of people, especially women, who will not take that trouble. Now that we have enfranchised women we ought to do everything we possibly c.an to make it easy for every woman who has a right to vote to be placed on the voters' Jist. Of course, if you provide that they may come on election day and swear in their vote, that is all right. But I know what the result will be because I was a scrutineer, under the old enumeration system a good- many times, and in my case-and in the case of every other scrutineer-when a person comes to ime whose name is not on the list, we simply say to the deputy returning officer, ''Give them every oath in the calendar"-that is the stereotyped phrase-and the result is that they have to take every oath provided for. Well, there are thousands of these women who, when they find they have to take every oath in the calendar will never go near the polling place. I do not think we should put them under any such disability. For my part I think the Government should have adhered to the original Bill; it was a whole lot better than what this reactionary conference has given us.

I object td the amendment because it is absolutely unfair to the people of the rural municipalities. In one province there is the possibility of appointing enumerators to go around from door to door and give the residents the privilege of having their names on the list. In another province that privilege is withheld and you accept as a basis for your Dominion list a provincial list that may be two years old. Then hundreds of people whose names may not be on the provincial list are obliged to watch for a sitting of the court and then go in person, it may be five, ten, fifteen or twenty miles, and make application for the privilege. I consider that is unfair. I know from personal experience what it means to have voters' lists revised, and I would like the minister to state who would be responsible for the revision of the lists in a province where a two years' old provincial list is accepted as a basis in the rural districts?

speechtext: I do not think I understand the question.

where you adopt the provincial list as a basis in rural constituencies you do not appoint enumerators. Then who is responsible to the individual elector or to the candidate, whoever he may be?

I mean those who are responsible. In one province you appoint enumerators that go around from door to door-

-and every man and woman has a right to have their names put on the list by the enumerator who calls at their residence.
