Putting ' the oath to
them is the only safeguard for which the Bill provides.

I am quite sure that my hon. friends opposite, as well as a great many hon. members on this side, do not for one moment realize the conditions which exist in the province of British Columbia. Without enumeration in that province, I venture to say that in the rural districts at least one-third of the electors would lose theii votes. We have no municipalities in the rural parts of British Columbia; they are practically all unorganized districts except in the villages. I want to say to the minister, and to this committee, that it would be most unfair to leave British Columbia in that position. I therefore strenuously oppose any amendment seeking to do away with the enumeration system as far as that province is concerned.

I am not sure
that I understand exactly what this proposition means, but so far as I can gather its purport it is this: That if in rural districts there are lists less than two years old there shall be no enumeration or registration. That would mean, if the lists were less than two years old, every man and woman on it would have to swear in order to be entitled to vote. I think the Minister of Immigration and Colonization knows what such a system as that would amount to as far as the province of Saskatchewan is concerned, and I can hardly imagine that he was at the conference referred to at which this amendment was adopted.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: That has been our system in Saskatchewan for several years past.

But we have had
(enumeration; now you propose to do away with that. I think I know what the result will be in the districts that I am acquainted with in the West. At one time the Saskatchewan Government ordered the list to be prepared every year. I presume my hon. friend (Mr. Calder) will remember that, too. That was done for two years in succession, and I recall that in my town I was acting for the Liberals and trying to revise the lists while a friend was acting for the Conservatives, and after we got through *twenty-five per cent -of the names were struck off the list and perhaps a little more

than twenty-five per cent added. I am satisfied, as regards several small towns in the West, that if you adopt the plan suggested by this amendment twenty-five per cent of the voters, in order to have their names placed on the list, will have to go and swear to the facts, with two persons to identify them. That means where you have one hundred voters to be added in a polling place, three hundred people will have to be on hand to swear to the correctness of the applications, and as my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Cowan) says the applicants are liable to have to swear to every oath on the list. I do not think the thing is practicable at all, and I cannot understand how my hon. friend (Mr. Calder) came to agree to it when he knows the conditions in the province of Saskatchewan so well.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
I was not"very far away when the committee was sitting, and at the time I thought the proposition was a very reasonable one. I am not just so certain of my view at this moment as a result of the discussion that has taken place. I wish to very briefly correct an impression that exists among some of the members on this side. When an enumeration takes place in the province of Saskatchewan it is not provided that the enumerator shall call at every house-that should be clearly understood. If the law provided that an enumerator should call at every house the expense would be enormous-in fact practically prohibitive. As a consequence of that our law has simply provided that the enumerator may, if he chooses, sit down in his own house and make out as good a list as he can from all the material that is available to him. There was a time, some eight or ten years ago, when we required the enumerator to make a house-to-house canvass, but that system was so expensive that we abolished it and adopted the other system under which the enumerator could take the municipal lists or any other material he found at hand and make out the very best list that he could. In addition to that, under the old federal law, as well as under our provincial law, there was always a provision that the voter whose name was not on the list could come forward on election day and swear in his vote. I must say after a great many years' experience with the working out of that law in Western Canada that while occasionally there may have been some slip, as a rule the law has been accepted by our people as workable and

fair, and so far as I am aware no serious criticism of it has come from any section of the community.
The real question that faces the committee and which we discussed the other day at our conference is whether or not it is possible to provide some means whereby the enormous cost of preparing lists under a system of enumeration can be avoided. Some take the view that it is better to put enumerators at work in order to get as complete a list as possible immediately prior to the election. Personally I am inclined to the other view; I think that if we can devise machinery which will enable us, looking at it from the federal standpoint, to prepare lists that are reasonably fair, then we should avoid the unnecessary expense of having the lists prepared by enumerators. In Saskatchewan and Alberta, if there have been provincial elections and lists have been prepared which are not more than two years old, we will accept those lists, not as final, but'merely as a basis for revision if they are available. In our urban communities there is machinery in the law for the revision of these lists immediately prior to the holding of a federal election. There is no reason why under this proposal every person who is qualified to vote in any of our cities or towns with a population of over one thousand should not have his name put on the list after the writs are issued. If, on the other hand, these provincial lists which are not more than two years old are loaded with the names of persons who are not qualified to vote when the federal election comes round, there is no reason why the lists should not be cleaned up in 'that regard as well. That position should be reasonably satisfactory to every one; there will be machinery for the obtaining of an up-to-date list immediately prior to the holding o*f a federal election. Now, as to the rural end of it, those lists prepared within the two year period would be used simply for what they are worth. They are there as a matter of record. Tt does not follow that any person whose name is on that list is entitled to vote or that any person whose name is not on the list is not entitled to vote. The list is merely to be used <as a convenience. It will not be revised in the sense that the city lists are to be revised; it will simply be handed to the deputy returning officer to be taken for what it is worth. Personally I have no objection to that provision so far as Saskatchewan is concerned so long as I know reasonable machinery is pro-166
vided which will enable any (man who is entitled to do so to oome forward on election day and put in his vote. That is all that we attempted to provide. Under the suggested- amendment notw before us provision is made whereby a rural voter whose name is not on the lilst -may apply, in the first place, to a judge and have his name added; or on election day he may have his -name added by having his qualification vouched for by two fellow-electors. I say frankly that I can quite understand how iit is that members from the East who are not fa-miliar with this- sort of law desire to have its provisions safeguarded. In the West we have had a law which enabled the man himself to -come forward on election day -and swear in his vote, -and we have never had any trouble with it. In Eastern Canada there are a good many people who are doubtful of the results of -a law of that hind land desire to throw -around at certain safeguards. Well, if the proposal made lis objectionable and some other safeguard -can be found that will be regarded as reasonable, then I think that the 'committee should endeavour to find that other safeguard.
The problem before the committee has two aspects. In the first place there are those who maintain that regardless of expense we should put an army of officials in the field immediately prior to an election for the purpose of getting the lists and, in the second place, there are those who. hold the view -that if it is possible to- do so-and it Would mean a saving of a 'million ,cxr a million and -a half dollars-we should endeavour to devise machinery whereby we could avoiid that expense. Personally I am -strongly inclined to the latter viewpoint. My good friend from East Edmonton (Mr. H. A. Mackie) speaks of (the enumerator. I know what the enumerator system is and I (think I may fairly say that -after observing the operation of 'that law as a member of the Provincial Government for fifteen years and watching las well the federal elections held out there, the appointment of enumerators -and the actions of enumerators do more harm to the Government that appoints them than they do to the other side. 'That is my experience; if I wanted to run an -election and had the ehotoe of appointing enumerators or letting the other fellow do- it, I would rather let the other fellow do it.
You are quite right.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
Because there is always a great deal olf -criticism -against that method



of 'building up lists. My own view is that if it is at all (possible to avoid that system we should do so*, especially if a good deal o!f money can be saved.

May I ask the Minister of Immigration a question? He hats made -a statement which is at variance with the statement made by the Acting Solicitor General, and that is the whole point of my remarks this afternoon. My objection is that we should take in Alberta as the basis of a federal election list :a list prepared by the enumerators, because I recognize the very thing 'that the minister recognizes-'that enumerators are not what they should be. But I isay that you should not force the provlinoial list upon us as the basis of .a federal election list; that is my whole objection. Now, I want to make sure about this. I asked the Acting Solicn

tor General: Is it not .a fact (that you said that the only list we are going to use as the basis of a federal election lis the provincial list which is going to be used as the list for provincial elections, and his answer is, yes. Well then, I say I have no Objection, -because in Alberta we have no such provincial lists. Every time there is an election, a new enumeration is made; but according to the amendment before the House, it is possible that the list prepared by the Provincial Government, which list is not one that they use themselves as a basis for the next election, will be the list which the Federal Government, if they hold an election within the period of two years of the making of this list, will be obliged to adopt, and you are forcing us to adopt a list made up by a class of men to whom you take exception. Iff you force us to accept a list made up by a class of men to whom you take exception, why do you object to our asking that you accept a list prepared in a similar manner? Who is right, the Minister of Immigration and'Colonization (Mr. Calder), or the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie)?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
After having
listened to what the Minister of Immigration and Colonization has said, it must he apparent to hem. members that those who were together when these suggestions were being discussed have, in regard to this whole matter, a point of view which it may be difficult for other hon. members to have who have not before them the exact amendments that are proposed. It is quite clear to those of us on both sides who discussed this matter that there are distinct merits in the suggestions which are to be moved,

if the committee so agrees, as amendments to the Bill as it stands, and I think the discussion, if we have regard to what has been said by different hon. members, discloses that many of the difficulties that are feared in what has been proposed, arise from the members not having before them the exact amendments as suggested. I know we are all anxious to get this legislation through as quickly as possible, and perhaps the quickest course to adopt would be for the minister to state to the committee the amendments he has in mind so that we shall have all the amendments before us and shall then be in a position to accept or reject them speedily. That would save a great deal of debate, and I am sure, if hon. members have an opportunity to consider these amendments from no point of view other than what is best for the country, what will give most confidence in an Election Act and what will avoid most extravagance and lessen the possibility of waste of public money, they will feel that what the Acting Solicitor General is about to suggest is most in accord with the public interest.

The argument on the
Opposition side of the House is that to adopt provincial lists as a basis for a federal list would mean a saving of a great deal of money to this country, hut I have not yet heard any hon. member point out how the saving would come about. For instance, each province has power to pass a Franchise Act regardless of the franchise qualifications in any other province. Let us assume for the purpose of argument that every province in the Dominion passes different qualifications, and that the Dominion passes a Franchise Act in which the qualifications are different from those of any one of the nine provinces. What would be the result? The result would be that persons who are charged with the preparation of the lists must satisfy themselves as regards every name which goes upon the federal list; and as regards the provincial list forming a basis for the preparation of the federal list, it cannot possibly be any better basis than a list compiled from a city directory or a telephone directory or a municipal list or any other lists of names of people living in the community in which the voters' list is being prepared. Let us assume that the Federal Act provides a residence qualification of twelve months in the district, and that the Provincial Act provides a residence qualification of six months in the district, and that in all other respects the franchise qualifications

agree. What does that mean? It means that we have, placed in the hands of the federal officers a list under which the qualification of residence is six months. Therefore, the federal officers must satisfy themselves as regards every man whose name is on the list. If we were at a Stage where the qualifications for the exercise of the franchise were uniform in the various provinces and in the Dominion as a whole, there might be no question as to adopting the provincial lists as the basis of our lists or as the real list of those who are entitled to exercise the Franchise in a Dominion election. But where the respective qualifications vary, it is absolutely necessary that the qualifications of every man whose name is on any list should be investigated to ascertain whether they conform with the requirements of the Federal Act under which he wishes to exercise the franchise. As a matter of practical economy, I cannot see where one dollar will be saved if justice is to be done in connection with the federal franchise.
If the Federal Franchise Act says So and So may vote and any province varies from that, in that province every name that goes on the federal list must be examined to see whether or not the man has, not the qualifications of the Provincial Act, but the qualifications of the Federal Act finder which he wishes to exercise the franchise. I should like to hear some hon. member explain where the real economy in this comes in. I am inclined to agree with my hon. .friend (Mr. H. A. Mackie) that what is at stake is really who is going to exercise the authority of preparing the list of voters to be used throughout the Dominion of Canada.
As regards the revision clause, I think 1 pointed out before that where any class of work is being done on behalf of the Federal Government or the Provincial Government, the officers who are performing that work are the servants of the Federal Government or the Provincial Government respectively. The Government would be ill advised to accept officers of another Government to perform duties in connection with its own Act. You must have the utmost harmony, and you can get that only when you appoint men who are subject to your jurisdiction and instruction. It is an anomaly for us to say that we shall have a Federal Franchise Act prepared for ourselves, and at the same time place the doing of that work in the hands of some persons who are not in any way responsible to this Government.
As regards the conduct of enumerators in Alberta, I must disagree with the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) who says that the lists used in the last election would be the basis of the federal lists. My understanding of the provincial enumeration list is that as soon as an election is held, the list becomes a nullity; it automatically dies under our Statute, because it is used only for the purpose of the particular election for which it was prepared. If we were to hold another election in Alberta three months later, we would still be required to prepare a new list by the method of enumeration, the old list being dead. I have always found that the enumeration method has worked out well in Alberta. There is no doubt that mistakes occur and perhaps once in a while you might find an enumerator who did not do his duty properly; but the practice has been that the enumerator goes from house to house in order to ascertain who are entitled to vote in the city or in the country; he can get that definite information only by going from house to house and office to office to ascertain that he gets the names of all those who are entitled to be on the lists.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
The Bill does not provide for enumeration in a city like Calgary.
As to the other point raised, the question of economy, at this very time the Manitoba Government is preparing lists for an election to be held in June or July. In the city of Winnipeg they have personal registration. Every elector must come forward and have his name put on the list. I suppose that will take probably three or four or five weeks. After that personal registration takes place, they must go through a form of revision, to strike off and put on. Let us assume they have completed their list and held a provincial election, and that we hold a federal election six months from now. Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that if we took that list which was completed only six months before, and merely revised it for the purpose of our federal election, that there would not be a large saving of money and a great saving of trouble and'expense on the part of the people? Notwithstanding the existence of that list, which so far as I am aware is based on exactly the same requirements as our list, as to residence, naturalization, and everything of that character, does he suggest that notwithstanding the expense to which the province of Manitoba has been put in the preparation of that list, we

should go to the trouble and expense of duplicating all that work, simply because the list was not prepared by the Federal Government? It seems to me that if we provide the necessary machinery to make certain that that list is not prepared from the ground up, but merely revised for the purpose of our election, we are bound to save a great deal of money and put our people to far less trouble and expense than they would otherwise be put to.

That is exactly the suggestion I intended to make. My point was that if the qualifications for voters throughout the various provinces were uniform with the federal requirements, that system could be carried out. But we have no control over the franchise of the provinces; they can make their own qualifications, and they may all be different at the present time, or, after we pass our Act, they might pass an Act which would be entirely repugnant to ours. My point is that where there is any variation between the provincial and the federal qualifications you cannot adopt the provincial lists, because you must investigate the qualifications of every voter on that list. The province may require a residence of six months in the province, two months in the constituency, and a month in the polling division, and the Federal Act, twelve months in the province, six months in the constituency, and two months in the polling subdivision. IThose are three distinct points. They exist at the present time in various provinces. What does that mean? Every one of those names must be investigated to see whether or not the voter has the qualifications which are required by the Federal Franchise Act, and they are not entitled to be put on. the federal list until that information has been gathered. It means that you could use the provincial list simply as a sort of index or directory, as a list of the names of people who might possibly have the qualifications. But it is the duty of the federal officers to go out and ascertain whether they have the qualifications required by the federal law, because they were placed on the provincial list under different qualifications.

Maybe I have been the unhappy cause of this discussion. JE did not intend to be. In the case mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Tweedie), the protection would be the swearing-in of the voter at the polls.

Does my hon. friend mean to suggest that every man who goes

to vote should have to take the oath?- You would not get the votes polled in a week in that case.

I am not contending that. The local officers would know whether they had the qualifications. That is not the point I rose to speak on. I have the amendment before me, suggested by the Acting Solicitor General, to carry out the views of the conference held on the 13th of May, and I think they are all an absolute improvement on the Act. I did not move any amendment at all, but simply threw out in good faith a suggestion to the committee. If the committee does not see fit to accept it, well and good.

I think we are pretty close to an agreement except on the one point as to the provision to be made for the rural votes. I am not at all satisfied with the amendment as it stands for taking care of the rural voters. I am of the opinion that it would be possible to provide that in the rural districts, just as in the city districts, there shall be opportunity for revision some days before polling day. I think if that could be done, we ought to be able to reach an agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I want to make it clear that I have not moved an amendment. I have made a suggestion, and the suggestion has certainly come from the conference which was held on Thursday last. I think it might not be out of the way if I followed the suggestion of the leader of the Opposition and let the committee know the exact language of what I suggest. I handed a copy of the document which I have in my hand to the chairman-of the committee, but I have not made any motion by way of amending section 32. The ideas of the conference of Thursday last, as reduced to writing by me, are about as follows. I may not have carried out all the views of those present, but I have tried to. There are one or two minor amendments to section 32 before we come to the schedules. I was going to propose that schedule 1, which is apparently a somewhat clumsy enactment as drawn in the Bill, be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
Rule (1). Immediately after the receipt of the writ the returning officer shall appoint, by writing, in Form E one person only to be registrar of voters in each city, town or incorporated village which is wholly or partially contained in the electoral district for which the election is pending and which has a population of over 1,000 or less than 4,000" persons, and one for each additional 4,000 persons, who shall, before acting as such, take the oath in Form F;

and the registrars so appointed shall be assigned by the returning officer to such parts or such number of polls as he may deem right and proper.
That is important only in regard to the number of registrars which we will have in urban districts. The next amendment of any consequence would be to schedule B, page 22, which is the schedule providing for the lists in rural polling divisions. I propose to strike out Rule 1 as printed, and insert instead the following:
Rule (1) No rural registrar shall be appointed in any electoral district in any province where provincial voters' lists are available for the purposes of a Dominion election under the provisions of subsection one of section thirty-two of this Act. In such cases provincial voters' lists shall be adopted as final and complete for rural polling divisions; subject, however, to the right of any person to apply to have his name added to the voters' list as provided by section sixty-three of this Act; and subject also to the right of any person resident in a rural polling division to apply in person to the revising officer of any urban polling division in the same electoral district, or if there be no urban polling division in such electoral district, to the nearest revising officer in another electoral district, to have his name added to the voters' list for such rural polling division; Such application may be made at any time during the sittings of such revising officer as provided by rule 13 of schedule A of the said section 32 ; and the revising officer to whom such application shall be so made, if satisfied that the applicant is a person qualified as an elector to vote at the election then pending within such rural polling division, may by writing under his hand addressed to the returning officer of the proper electoral district, order that the name of such person be added to the voters' list for the proper rural polling division. The revising officer shall thereafter, and not later than the twelfth day before polling day, deliver or send by registered mail to each returning officer and to each candidate in each of the electoral districts affected thereby, a list of all persons added to the voters' lists giving the names, residences and additions of such persons and designating the rural polling divisions in which such names have been so added to the voters' lists. The returning officer shall thereupon and in due time before polling day notify the deputy returning officers in each rural polling division affected of the names, residences and additions of the persons so added to the voters' lists by the revising officer. For the purposes of this rule the method of procedure and the powers and authority of the revising officer shall be similar to those set forth in Rules 14 and 15 of Schedule A to the said section thirty-two.
That would be rule (1). Then the present rule (1) I would merely amend in the first few lines as follows;-
If under the laws of any province no provincial voters' lists exist which are available for the purposes of a Dominion election under the provisions of subsection (1) of section 32 of this Act, the returning officer shall, immediately after the receipt of the writ, appoint by writing in Form E one person only to be registrar of voters for each polling division. Whenever a competent person can be secured-
And add the words:
-who is a resident within the limits of the polling division, such person shall be appointed, and only in case of necessity shall a registrar be selected from an outside polling division.
Then I would also suggest that another rule be added to Rule B to be known as 4 A, or to be renumbered after the clause is passed, in the following words:
Any person claiming to be an elector who is dissatisfied with any decision of a registrar under the last preceding rule may apply to the revising officer of any urban polling division in the electoral district wherein such person resides in the same manner as provided under Rule (1) of this Schedule and such revising officer may hear and determine such application, and may order, notify and report upon the same in the same manner and to the same end as provided under the said Rule (1).
Then I would add another rule as No. 4-B:
Any person who has applied either under Rule (1) or Rule (4) of this schedule to a revising officer to have his name added to the voters' list and whose application has been refused by such revising officer shall not thereafter be entitled to apply to have his name added to the voters' list under the provisions of section sixty-three of this Act. If any person, after such refusal by a revising officer, as aforesaid, shall require or request any deputy returning officer to add such person's name to the voters' list under the provisions of section sixty-three of this Act, such person shall be guilty of an offense under this Act and shall be punishable therefor as provided by section eighty-five of this Act.
Then I make provision for the amendment of subsection (1) of section 32 by changing the term "one year" into "two years" in regard to provincial voters' lists. And it would be necessary to make some amendments to section 33 by adding at the end of subsection (2) the following in regard to voters' lists, that is, where an election has taken place and the lists have been returned to the Chief Electoral Officer and a new election is called:
And the same-
Meaning the voters' lists.
-shall thereafter he completed, revised and distributed as provided by Schedules A and B respectively to section 32 of this Act.
Then I would suggest that subsection 3 and 4 be struck out.
It would be necessary also to bring section 63 into conformity with the provisions which I have just read. Therefore, if my suggestions were met, I would propose to amend section 63, subsection (I) as follows :
At polling stations in rural polling divisions the deputy returning officer shall, while the poi] is open, if required by any person whose

name is not on the voters' list and who is vouched for by two electors who are resident in such polling division, administer to such person oath number (1) in form "Z" No. 1 of schedule 1 to this Act and to each of such other two persons an oath in form "Z" No. 2 of schedule 1 to this Act, and such oath having been taken by the applicant person and by such two other persons, the deputy returning officer shall at once cause such applicant person's name to be added to the voters' list, with the word "sworn" written thereafter, and subject to the next following subsection of this Act, such applicant person may thereupon vote.
I would add to the next following subsection, which is subsection (2) by inserting in line 30 after the word "make" the following words:
including the names of the two persons who vouched for the applicant person.
I have also prepared a form of oath to be taken by the two persons who act as sureties or vouchers for the persons whose names are so added, which is practically a repetition of the oath of the elector, that they know the elector, and they know and state his qualifications to vote at the election. That, I think, would make more certain that this privilege of voting under section 63 would not be abused.
Then, as I intimated a few moments ago, I would suggest that section 100 be amended by striking out the words "or other persons" in the first line. That would confine the section in its application to railway men, sailors and commercial travellers.
These are the amendments which were in my mind, suggested as a result of the conference which we held on Wednesday. I have given them now to the committee in order that hon. members may fully understand the scope of them; but it must be borne in mind that I have not yet moved them as amendments.

One or two features of this Franchise Act appealed, I think, to almost every member when it was introduced. One was that we were to have valid up-to-date lists, a matter in which the rural constituencies have suffered for many years as compared with the urban constituencies. Representing a rural constituency as I do, I think it is a most important feature of the Bill that rural lists should he up-to-date-even more important,
I think, than that the urban lists should be up-to-date.
Another feature which commended itself to me was the simplicity of the machinery prescribed for the preparation of the lists. Perhaps it is expensive. Those of us who have had to do with the preparation and

revision of these lists in years past know that the old method in Ontario was exceedingly expensive,-especially to the candidates. We cannot have an accurate up-to-date list without expense. It is a question whether the Government should bear the expense or whether the individual candidates themselves should bear it. After the discussion to-day, and especially after the reading of the Acting Solicitor General's proposed amendments, I have lost my vision of up-to-date lists for the rural constituencies and a simple method of preparing those lists. Franchise Acts in the past have been very confusing to the average man. But I do not think I have ever heard or read of any provisions which were proposed for a franchise Bill which would be more confusing to an ordinary elector than the proposals now laid before the nouse by the Acting Solicitor General, and if these are the best fruits of a conference, then I would say do away with conferences and leave the matter in the hands of this committee, which could decide perhaps more promptly and with better results what the provisions of the Act should be. Many members probably do not appreciate what it would mean to adopt this method of preparing the lists in rural constituencies. Three or four years ago I made an estimate of the changes which would be made in my own constituency, which is a very small and stable one ; there not being many people coming and going. I found about 450 names of new voters on one list as compared with the previous list. That probably is about the average number of changes that take place each year. If we were using a list two years old containing the names of the old electorate and when the women were not included there would probably be a thousand changes. With the women added we would probably have 2,000 new voters. What does it mean when we enter an election campaign to have 2,000 people who are entitled to vote but whose names are not on the list? This amendment provides for people going to some revising officer somewhere and having their names added. If they do not do that they can go up on election day and swear in their votes. Just imagine what that would mean in my small constituency. I venture to say that in North Perth there would be 'from 4,000 to 6,000 voters whose names would not be on a two-year-old list when the election campaign came on. It seems to me that a statement of this kind is sufficient to let the House see that the system is practically unworkable. The result will be that if that

system is followed there will be hundreds of men and women who will be deprived of the right of voting or who will have to go to the polls on election day and swear in their votes. The polling booths will be so congested from morning till night that there will be ill feeling, disturbance and uncertainty at the polls. I sincerely trust that the Acting Solicitor General will return to the original clause, even if it is necessary to make some amendment to meet the question of expense. I think that would be very desirable. I do not see why we should not have in any rural constituency the same system which is adopted in an urban constituency. Have a revising officer in each municipality, and if there are names on the list which should not be there the necessary changes can be made by the revising officer. That would simplify it very much. Voters would know exactly where they had to go and what they had to do, while under the proposed amendment the confusion will be very great because so many people will desire to have their names put on the list.

I understand that a voter in a rural district who is not on the revised list would have the right to vote if the revising officer in some town should add his name. If the revising officer should refuse, would he still have the right to have his name put oni the list by a judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If he does he will commit an offence which under the Act is punishable. The presumption is that the judge will inquire into the matter and decide whether he has the right to vote or not.
Then the revising officer is the final court of appeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Why should there be an appeal in the urban district and not in the rural?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is the same.
You have an appeal to the judge in the urban district.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: A man in the rural district, under the amendment, has an appeal to the same judge.

That is what I
was asking you. I understood he would not have.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, and the decision of the judge will be final in both instances. But if a man in a rural district should attempt to swear himself in he will be liable under the Act.
The hon. gentleman misunderstood my question. I understand the applicant has an appeal to a judge and that if the judge decides that he is not entitled to vote, he must not swear his name in?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.

With regard to
swearing on the name, I concur in what the hon. the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) says, that where the practice has been tried it has been found thoroughly satisfactory. I think that is the agreement of hon. members on both sides of the House who. know anything about it. I think it is the best and safest plan you could possibly adopt, and to do away with it is a most dangerous thing.
In the application of the law is a voter's oath alone taken as sufficient?
Yes.
Has that been quite satisfactory without having the oaths of two resident electors?

I am quite willing to accept that because apparently hon. gentlemen who do not know how the system is actually working in the province of Saskatchewan are frightened. It has been found satisfactory there. But let us have the addition which the Acting Solicitor General has suggested because it may be that people in other provinces, being unfamiliar with the system, are suspicious of it. But do not shut out the right of a man to record his vote by that method in a rural district because if you do you are going to shut out a great many votes.

I am not sure that the amendment is going to be workable in country districts. Where a Dominion election was held within two years after the provincial list had been revised, the electors would have no means of placing their names on the list except by making application to a judge or enumerator in a town where there were
2,000	inhabitants. In a large country constituency, such as I represent, I fancy this would be practically impossible. Where the vote is changed so quickly and where a great many new voters are coming in I fancy the Act would be entirely unworkable. It we had 300 names on the list in a polling subdivision and it should be necessary to swear in fifty, sixty or a hundred more, I cannot see how it could be done unless we

created double polls in each polling subdivision. It would be practically impossible to get the vote polled in the time allowed for the polling to take place. As far as I can see a thorough revision of the lists in the country constituencies is necessary previous to an election, especially where those lists are two years old. I cannot see any other procedure to follow that would give justice to the people living in the country; and in my opinion it would be a mistake to adopt any amendment that would tend to disfranchise great numbers of these electors. Probably hon. members who represent constituencies in the East have no idea of the size of our western constituencies. For example, my constituency is something like three hundred miles long by one hundred and fifty miles wide, and it would be out of the question for many persons to travel such a great distance to register in any town or village. Yet their only means of getting their names on the list would be on polling day, and they would be compelled to bring two of their neighbours a very great distance to give evidence that they were properly qualified. Therefore I think some other method should 'be adopted whereby registration can take place in our rural constituencies. I would like the committee to carefully consider these matters because they affect the western constituencies in a very important manner.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

communications with the United States. It is important in its hearing on our relations with the Mother Country. For all these -reasons, on an important matter, on a matter which is not urgent nor pressing, on -a matter which affords every opportunity for preliminary consideration and reflection, it would be -a wise policy for the Government to halt in their proceedings, and before they go further, to bring the whole matter fully before the Parliament of Canada, in order that We may be able to exercise sound judgment on the -subject.
